name: Damon self-ligating braces

lead: Damon braces are orthodontic brackets that hold the archwire with a built-in sliding door instead of rubber ties. People choose them for straighter teeth and a broader, fuller-looking smile, and the system is marketed for expanding the arch without extractions.

The passive clip lets the wire slide with little friction, so teeth move under lighter forces as the wire shape guides alignment. Systematic reviews describe lower friction as the most consistent advantage, with mixed findings on treatment time, comfort and hygiene. Looksmax forum users credit the system with arch expansion and, in some posts, jaw changes; no trials show facial-bone change from the bracket type.

paras: Treatment is run by an orthodontist as a standard course of braces: brackets bonded to the teeth, a series of archwires, and regular adjustment visits over many months. Users typically pair it with a retainer afterwards to hold the result.

Risks are those of braces generally: tooth soreness, mouth irritation, decalcification or decay if cleaning is poor, and relapse without a retainer. Reviews do not link the bracket type to extra hygiene problems. Claims of jaw or maxilla change have not been studied.

angle.text: The payoff people want is a straighter, fuller smile. Self-ligating brackets move the teeth under light forces, broadening the arch and aligning them, and forum users credit the system with extra arch expansion. Reviews report lower friction as the main documented advantage.

lead: Damon braces are a line of self-ligating orthodontic brackets, which hold the archwire with a built-in sliding door instead of elastic ties. They are used to align crowded or rotated teeth and to straighten the smile. The Damon SL1 was introduced in 1996 and is classed as a passive self-ligating system.[1] Manufacturers and some orthodontists say the design reduces friction and allows lighter forces, and the system is often marketed for arch expansion without extractions.

On looksmax.org, Damon braces are discussed as a way to widen the dental arch, improve the smile and, according to some posters, support jaw development. Published reviews describe a more modest picture: friction is the most consistently reported advantage in laboratory conditions, while claims about faster treatment, comfort and hygiene are mixed or unsupported.[1]

Controlled studies of the Damon system generally report that teeth align and the arches widen with treatment, and that the amount of widening is similar to that seen with conventional brackets.[2][3][4][5]
infobox: Passive self-ligating (door does not press on wire)[1]

paras: Self-ligating brackets are typically stainless steel, though ceramic and polycarbonate versions exist, and are divided into passive types, where the door applies no pressure on the wire, and active types, where a clip presses on it. Damon brackets are passive.[1] Advocates cite fewer elastic ties, a smaller appearance and shorter appointments.[1]

Passive systems aim for low friction between slot and wire, and a 2010 study cited on Wikipedia found lower static and kinetic friction for passive than active self-ligating brackets with a 0.019 by 0.025 inch stainless steel wire.[1] The Damon lineage runs from the SL1 (1996) through the Twinlock bracket by A.J. Wildman, marketed by Ormco from 1998 and later renamed Damon 2 (2000), to the Damon 3, a metal and composite hybrid introduced in 2004.[1]

The Damon system is promoted as a combined bracket and treatment approach that uses light, continuous forces with highly flexible wires and often little or no extraction. Proponents describe it as widening the arch, relieving crowding and giving a fuller smile; the 2019 systematic review of Damon philosophy tests this by comparing skeletal and dentoalveolar changes with conventional techniques.[2]

The phrase "lip bumper effect" has been used in the orthodontic literature to describe a claimed arch-widening action in which cheek and lip muscle forces are balanced by the passive bracket and flexible wires. A 2011 controlled study set out to test this claim.[5]

A 2016 meta-analysis found no hygiene or discomfort advantage for self-ligating brackets over conventional ones, and a 2016 review found no significant difference in periodontal status, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] A 2010 review supported only shorter chair time and slightly less incisor proclination, while another analysis reported longer treatment times with self-ligating brackets.[1] A 2009 review found lower friction with small round wires in well-aligned arches but insufficient evidence for large rectangular wires.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed three-appliance trial (n=96, 2009 start) and a trial of Damon versus MBT brackets measuring compliance and treatment efficiency (n=34, active in 2025).[6][7] Results are not reported in the registry entries examined here. No trial examined whether Damon braces change facial structure.

A 2019 systematic review of seven controlled studies compared skeletal and dentoalveolar changes with the Damon system against conventional treatment. Most studies found an increase in maxillary intercanine, interpremolar and intermolar distance after treatment in both the Damon and comparison groups, and all concluded that the final transverse dimension did not differ significantly between them.[2]

A 2018 randomised trial in Buenos Aires treated 24 patients aged 13 to 36 with 4 to 6 mm of crowding, 12 with Damon and 12 with conventional Roth brackets, and measured dental casts after alignment. Both systems increased transverse arch diameter; the distance between upper first premolars and between canines rose more in the conventional group.[3]

A 2014 randomised comparison in 33 adolescents with Class I maxillary constriction compared Roth brackets after quad-helix expansion (17 patients) with the Damon 3MX system (16 patients). Both groups showed increased intercanine, interpremolar and intermolar widths and proclined incisors; the Damon group had a greater increase in maxillary molar inclination, and periodontal index and pain score changes did not differ.[4]

A 2011 controlled study compared 27 patients treated with the Damon system with 16 treated with conventional edgewise brackets. It found that the claimed lip bumper effect was not supported, with similar crowding relief, transverse expansion and incisor advancement in both groups.[5]

A 2014 randomised trial of 22 patients aged 16 to 30 compared gingival response in Damon and Roth brackets, and found no statistically significant difference in plaque, gingival or probing-depth indices between groups, although indices rose at 14 days, particularly with self-ligating brackets.[8] A 2016 retrospective study of 52 patients compared external apical root resorption with Damon and conventional preadjusted appliances.[9]

Forum posters often present Damon braces as preferable to conventional braces and Invisalign for arch expansion and smile aesthetics, and some link them to jaw development, nasal breathing and "mewing". Users commonly ask whether they affect the upper jaw (maxilla), with some replies saying they allow continued growth rather than directly changing the bone.

Risks are those of fixed braces generally, such as gum irritation, plaque accumulation and root resorption, and the reviewed trials do not show a hygiene or comfort difference by bracket type.[1][8][9] Case reports describe the Damon system being used in complex situations such as temporomandibular dysfunction, and studies have examined it alongside piezocision surgery, but these are not trials of facial change.[10]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org threads describe Damon braces as the best bracket type for arch widening and facial harmony, often alongside palate expanders.
